docs.title: flinch
docs.text:
Solar flares in Sun-as-a-star radial velocities.

Do solar flares contaminate the radial-velocity detection of Earth analogues?

To find a planet like the Earth around a star like the Sun, the velocity of the star has to be measured to about 10 cm/s: the Earth moves the Sun by 9 cm/s. Some of the spectrographs built for that also observe the Sun every clear day, as if it were a distant star. This project cross-matches those solar velocities with the flares recorded by the GOES satellites and asks:

  1. Does a flare move the radial velocity of the Sun seen as a star?
  2. From which flare size, and by how much?
  3. What does that mean for planet searches?

It uses two instruments that watch the Sun at different hours and therefore see different flares: NEID (Arizona) and HARPS-N (La Palma).

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
Solar flares do not significantly contaminate the detection of Earth analogues by radial velocity. This has been shown for the Sun, not for Sun-like stars in general.

Question Answer Evidence Does the velocity change during a flare? No, within 7 cm/s 254 measurements of 253 flares of class M and X: −0.029 ± 0.026 m/s. NEID alone: −0.035 ± 0.035 (139 flares). HARPS-N alone: −0.021 ± 0.039 (115) Do larger flares move it more? No 18 flares of class X: −0.074 ± 0.072 m/s. No change, but the limit, 0.2 m/s, is twice the signal of the Earth Is there a rotation signature (opposite sign east and west)? No −0.006 ± 0.038 m/s for an X1 flare at the limb, within a factor of 1.6 to 3.5 of the largest shift expected Would a signal have been seen? Yes 98 % of a shift added to the data is measured back Do the spectra see the flares at all? Yes Ca II H and K and H alpha brighten in all 14 flares on the disc with spectra, by 2 to 5 parts per thousand How much of the time is the Sun flaring? 1.6 % 358 flares of class M or X per year on average from 2020 to 2026, counted from start to end (19 minutes in the median); 3.8 % in 2024, the most active year

The Sun does not flinch, but it blushes: the chromospheric lines brighten while the velocity stays put. See Results.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The package needs Python 3.10 or later.

git clone https://github.com/gabgarar/flinch.git
cd flinch
python -m venv venv
venv/Scripts/python -m pip install -e ".[analysis,dev]"     # Windows
venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[analysis,dev]"         # Linux and macOS

The distribution is called flinch-rv (the name flinch is taken on PyPI by an unrelated package); the import name is flinch.

Extra Adds Needed for analysis SciPy, Matplotlib, Astropy Figures, line shapes, reading the spectra dev pytest The tests docs mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings, mkdocs-static-i18n Building this site notebooks ipykernel Notebooks

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
Everything runs through python -m flinch <command>.

Command What it does Time Download download Everything the velocity analysis needs: flare lists, positions and one-minute fluxes (GOES), and the velocities of NEID and HARPS-N 3 min 340 MB coverage Which flares happened while NEID was observing seconds none replication The velocity measurement with NEID and with HARPS-N, and both together 20 s none robustness The NEID result under other windows, backgrounds and controls 10 s none pilot The first NEID analysis, with the oscillation power 10 s none numbers The counts and descriptive numbers of the text 5 s none spectra Extracts of every spectrum in a time window 10 s per spectrum 113 MB per spectrum campaign Unattended spectra for the strongest flares, or for their control windows hours 113 MB per spectrum paper-spectra Exactly the 1296 spectra of the paper, each checked against its fingerprint 3 hours or more 143 GB chromosphere Response of the spectral indices to the flares with spectra 1 min none paper-figures The figures of the paper, as PDF in journal style 20 s none verify Every number of the paper against the tables in results/ seconds none reproduce All of the above in order, with a report of what agrees (see Reproducing the paper) 10 min 340 MB, or 143 GB more with the spectra

A first session:

python -m flinch download
python -m flinch coverage
python -m flinch replication
python -m pytest

docs.title: Where the data go
docs.text:
Downloads go to data/ inside the repository, or to the folder named by the environment variable FLINCH_DATA. Tables go to results/, or to the folder named by FLINCH_RESULTS, and figures to docs/web/img/. reproduce writes everything to reproduction/ and leaves the repository as it was.

Flares and observations after 12 November 2026 are ignored, so that a later download gives the same sample (why).

Spectra are heavy to download

A level-2 NEID spectrum is 113 MB and the archive does not serve byte ranges, so each one is downloaded whole, reduced to a 0.2 MB extract and deleted. The 1296 spectra of the paper move 143 GB through the network and keep 260 MB. The computer must stay awake: on a laptop, keep it plugged in and with the lid open.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
python -m pytest

The tests use synthetic data and do not touch the network.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
The measurement has four steps. The figure shows them for one flare.

Left: the X1.3 flare of 30 March 2022. Right: one of its control days, the same hour a day later. Top: X-ray flux. Bottom: NEID velocities after removing the trend of the day, one point per spectrum. The grey band is the window before the flare and the blue band the window during its rise; the thick lines are the mean velocity in each. One flare or one control changes by tens of cm/s by chance; only the average over many flares, compared with their controls, reaches the precision needed.

  1. Clean the velocities: drop those taken through clouds and remove the slow trend of each day.
  2. For each flare, take the mean velocity during its rise minus the mean velocity just before it.
  3. Repeat step 2 on days without flares, at the same hour (the controls), and subtract their mean change from that of the flare.
  4. Average over all the flares.

docs.title: Step 1: cleaning the velocities
docs.text:
A cloud that covers part of the rotating disc shifts the velocity by tens of m/s. For NEID a spectrum is kept when its signal-to-noise ratio is within 1 % of that of its neighbours, its velocity error is below 1 m/s and its velocity is within five standard deviations of the trend of the day. For HARPS-N the quality flag of its data release is used (above 0.99).

The velocity drifts slowly through the day, because of the rotation of the Earth and of the changing height of the Sun. A polynomial of degree 2 is fitted to each day and subtracted. Days with too few good velocities, or with a scatter above 1.5 m/s, are dropped.

NEID HARPS-N Velocities kept 233 857 93 593 Days 1238 1671 Scatter of one velocity 0.81 m/s 0.44 m/s

Details in NEID velocities and HARPS-N velocities.

docs.title: Step 2: the velocity change of a flare
docs.text:
Window Limits Before From 40 to 5 minutes before the start of the flare During From the start to 2 minutes after the X-ray peak (the rise of the flare)

Δv = mean velocity during − mean velocity before

A flare counts only if both windows hold at least 70 % of the velocities expected.

Step NEID HARPS-N M and X flares in the years of the instrument 2122 1750 With both windows complete 140 122 With at least three controls 139 115

docs.title: Step 3: the controls
docs.text:
The velocity of the Sun changes all the time, flare or no flare. To know what a flare adds, the same two windows are measured on other days at the same hour, up to 15 days before and after, with no M or X flare within 45 minutes. Shifting by whole days keeps the height of the Sun and the daily cycle of the instrument.

d = Δv of the flare − mean Δv of its controls

If flares do nothing to the velocity, d averages to zero.

docs.title: Step 4: averages
docs.text:
Number Definition What it tests Mean change Mean of d Any shift common to the flares Shift of an X1 flare, S Σ f d / Σ f² A shift that grows with the size of the flare Rotation term, R Σ (f v) d / Σ (f v)² A shift with the sign of the side of the disc

f is the size of the flare, its peak flux in units of X1 (0.1 for M1, 2 for X2). v is its position: the rotation velocity at the flare as a fraction of that at the limb (−1 at the east limb, +1 at the west limb).

The rotation term is the one test whose sign can be predicted. A flare is a bright patch on a rotating disc, so it should shift the velocity by

shift ≈ (ΔF / F) · v_rot · K

where ΔF / F is the fraction by which the flare brightens the Sun in visible light, v_rot the rotation velocity at the flare (up to 1845 m/s at the limb, as seen from the Earth) and K a factor between 0 and 1. K is 1 if the extra light carries the same absorption lines as the surface under it, and 0 if it is light without lines, which only makes the lines of the rest of the disc shallower.

docs.title: Errors, limits and sensitivity
docs.text:
• Errors. Flares of the same day are not independent. The calculation is repeated thousands of times with a random selection of the observing days (a bootstrap); the spread of the results is the error.
  • Limits. When a result x with error σ is compatible with zero, the largest value it could hide with 95 % confidence is |x| + 1.645 σ.
  • Two instruments. They are combined by weighting each with the inverse of the square of its error.
  • Sensitivity. A known shift is added to the published velocities during the "during" window of control epochs, and the whole measurement is repeated.

docs.title: The spectra
docs.text: Each NEID spectrum comes with indices that measure how bright the cores of chromospheric lines are. The response of an index to a flare is its mean from 8 minutes before the X-ray peak to 10 minutes after it, minus its mean before the start. The same is measured in control windows. See NEID spectra.

docs.title: What was fixed when
docs.text: The quality cuts were chosen from the noise of the controls and the number of flares, never from the result. The windows were fixed after a first look at the NEID data, not before; the robustness table shows the result with the alternatives. HARPS-N was analysed afterwards, once, with the choices already made.

docs.title: Flares in Sun-as-a-star spectra and velocities
docs.text:
• Pietrow, A. G. M., et al. (2024). A comparative study of two X2.2 and X9.3 solar flares observed with HARPS-N. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 682, A46.
  • Dumusque, X., et al. (2026). A decade of solar high-fidelity spectroscopy and precise radial velocities from HARPS-N. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 706, A231. The data release used here as second instrument. It cites Pietrow et al. (2024) as having shown that flares contribute negligibly to the velocity of quiet Sun-like stars; their limit was 50 cm/s, more than five times the signal of the Earth.
  • Dumusque, X., et al. (2021). Three years of HARPS-N high-resolution spectroscopy and precise radial velocity data for the Sun. Astronomy & Astrophysics.
  • Ma, Y. L., et al. (2024). Sun-as-a-star study of an X-class solar flare with spectroscopic observations of CHASE. The Astrophysical Journal, 966, 45.
  • Otsu, T., et al. (2022). Sun-as-a-star analyses of various solar active events using H alpha spectral images taken by SMART/SDDI. The Astrophysical Journal, 939, 98.
  • Otsu, T., et al. (2024). Sun-as-a-star analysis of the X1.6 flare on 2023 August 5: dynamics of postflare loops in spatially integrated observational data. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 974, L13.
  • Otsu, T., et al. (2026). Statistical study of the timing of the appearance of H alpha postflare loops: simple scaling law based on radiative cooling. The Astrophysical Journal, 997, 286.
  • Liu, X., et al. (2025). Sun-as-a-star analysis of the solar eruption source region using H alpha spectroscopic observations of CHASE. The Astrophysical Journal, 993, 126.
  • Yu, H. C., et al. (2025). Sun-as-a-star analysis of simulated solar flares. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 694, A315.
  • De Wilde, M., et al. (2025). Synthesizing Sun-as-a-star flare spectra from high-resolution solar observations. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 700, A275.
  • Zhang, J., et al. (2026). Can we distinguish the source region location of filament/prominence eruptions from the Sun-as-a-star H alpha spectrum? The Astrophysical Journal, 1004, 66.
  • Xu, Y., et al. (2022). Sun-as-a-star spectroscopic observations of the line-of-sight velocity of a solar eruption on 2021 October 28. The Astrophysical Journal, 931, 76.
  • Lu, H.-P., et al. (2023). Full velocities and propagation directions of coronal mass ejections inferred from simultaneous full-disk imaging and Sun-as-a-star spectroscopic observations. The Astrophysical Journal, 953, 68.

These are studies of single events, of a few events or of simulations, most of them in H alpha from imaging spectrographs: the spectra are integrated over a region around the flare and normalised by the light of the disc. Otsu et al. (2026) gather 34 flares, but measure in images when the postflare loops appear. Only the first of the list above measures radial velocities, for two flares: an upper limit of 50 cm/s and a request for a statistical follow-up. The last two measure, in extreme-ultraviolet lines, the velocity of the material ejected in eruptions (about 400 km/s along the line of sight in the event of Xu et al., and eight ejections in twelve years of data in Lu et al.). That is the velocity of the ejecta, not of the photospheric spectrum from which the radial velocity of a star is measured.

docs.title: Flares in the brightness of the Sun
docs.text:
• Kretzschmar, M., et al. (2010). The effect of flares on total solar irradiance. Nature Physics, 6, 690.
  • Kretzschmar, M. (2011). The Sun as a star: observations of white-light flares. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 530, A84.

docs.title: Flares and the global oscillations of the Sun
docs.text:
• Karoff, C., & Kjeldsen, H. (2008). Evidence that solar flares drive global oscillations in the Sun. The Astrophysical Journal, 678, L73.
  • Kumar, B., et al. (2010). On the flare induced high-frequency global waves in the Sun. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 711, L12.
  • Kumar, B., et al. (2017). On the signatures of flare-induced global waves in the Sun: GOLF and VIRGO observations. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 471, 4677.
  • Richardson, M., Hill, F., & Stassun, K. G. (2012). No evidence supporting flare-driven high-frequency global oscillations. Solar Physics, 281, 21.

docs.title: Velocities inside the flaring area
docs.text:
These works look at the velocity where the flare is, in resolved images or in simulations, not at the velocity of the whole disc.

  • Saar, S. H., Palumbo, M. L., Haywood, R. D., & Dupree, A. K. (2018). A first look at the effect of flares on radial velocity jitter in G dwarfs: a punch and a splash? Poster at Cool Stars 20, doi:10.5281/zenodo.1490103. Pixels flagged as flares in SDO images of 2014 (more than four times as bright as the quiet Sun at 170 nm) are shifted by about 160 m/s to the red near the disc centre and by 130 to 220 m/s to the blue near the limb. Over the year they cover 0.04 % of the disc, and in the authors' tentative model only 29 % of them follow the catalogued flares.
  • Monson, A. J., et al. (2021). Flare-induced photospheric velocity diagnostics. The Astrophysical Journal, 915, 16. Simulations: chromospheric emission makes photospheric Fe I lines look shifted by up to 40 m/s.

docs.title: Solar rotation
docs.text: • Snodgrass, H. B., & Ulrich, R. K. (1990). Rotation of Doppler features in the solar photosphere. The Astrophysical Journal, 351, 309.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• NEID solar data. NEID Archive at the NASA Exoplanet Science Institute (NExScI), https://neid.ipac.caltech.edu.
  • HARPS-N solar data. Ten-year data release on the DACE platform of the University of Geneva, https://dace.unige.ch/sun/.
  • GOES-R XRS. Science-quality level-2 products of the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, https://data.ngdc.noaa.gov/platforms/solar-space-observing-satellites/goes/.

Note

The papers by Pietrow et al. (2024), Otsu et al. (2022, 2024, 2026), Kretzschmar (2010, 2011) and Dumusque et al. (2026) have been read in full. Two more were checked for the one thing they are cited for: the rotation rate in Table 1 of Snodgrass & Ulrich (1990), and the quality flag in Sect. 2.3 of Collier Cameron et al. (2019). The rest of the list rests on their abstracts.

docs.title: Reproducing the paper
docs.text:
One command downloads the public data, runs the whole analysis, compares every table with the one kept in the repository and checks every number of the paper against the new tables.

python -m flinch reproduce

It needs 340 MB of downloads and about ten minutes. It leaves the spectra out, which are 143 GB; the levels below say how to include them. Nothing in the repository is modified. The new tables, the figures, the output of every step and a report go to reproduction/.

Since 24 November 2026

NOAA has reissued the GOES files, so a download made now is no longer the one of the paper. The command still finds the 255 numbers of the paper in agreement, but it reports two inputs as different and five tables as DIFFERENT, and its last line is Not fully reproduced. The reissue of the GOES files says what changed and how to get the tables of the paper exactly.

docs.title: From zero
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/gabgarar/flinch.git
cd flinch
python -m venv venv
venv/Scripts/python -m pip install -r requirements-lock.txt     # the exact versions used
venv/Scripts/python -m pip install --no-deps -e .
venv/Scripts/python -m flinch reproduce

On Linux and macOS the interpreter is venv/bin/python. The paper was computed with Python 3.14 on Windows 11. Without the first pip line, pip install -e ".[analysis,dev]" installs the current versions instead, which is fine for using the package but is not the same test.

docs.title: Four levels
docs.text:
Each level adds a download to the one before.

Level Command Download Time What it shows 0 python -m flinch verify none seconds The numbers of the paper are those of the tables in the repository 1 python -m flinch reproduce 340 MB 10 min The public archives and this code give the 14 velocity tables again 2 python -m flinch reproduce --spectra sample 1.1 GB more 5 min more Ten spectra of the paper, drawn at random, are still the same in the archive 3 python -m flinch reproduce --spectra all 143 GB more 3 hours or more The spectral tables too: Tables 2 and B.1 and Fig. 4 of the paper

--sample 30 changes the number of spectra of level 2. --no-download uses the data already on disk. --out names another folder for the output. A run that is stopped can be started again, and what is on disk is not downloaded twice.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
reproduction/report.txt has six parts.

  1. Data. Each input is compared with the one used in the paper by a fingerprint (SHA-256) of what the analysis reads from it. identical means that the archive still serves the same data.
  2. Velocity analysis. One line per command, with the time it took and the file that keeps its output.
  3. Spectra. How many extracts are identical to those of the paper, and whether the spectral analysis was repeated.
  4. Figures. The figures of the paper, as PDF, in reproduction/figures/.
  5. Tables. Each new table against the one in the repository. identical is the same text. same numbers means that every number agrees to nine significant digits, which is what another processor or another version of a library can change. The response of the spectra is written in parts per thousand or per million of each quantity, and there the nine digits are those of the quantity. DIFFERENT names the columns that differ and by how much.
  6. Numbers of the paper. The 255 numbers of the text and the tables of the paper, each against the new tables. A number passes when the paper gives a correct rounding of it.

The last line is Reproduced. when no step failed, no table differs and every number agrees. The command then ends with code 0, and with 1 otherwise.

results/paper_check.csv lists the 255 numbers with the place where each appears in the paper, as the last run of verify left them.

docs.title: What was run for the paper
docs.text:
On 21 and 22 November 2026 everything was downloaded again into an empty folder and run from a fresh clone, with the versions of requirements-lock.txt.

What Result Inputs of the velocity analysis (12 files) identical, 12 of 12 Velocity tables (14) identical, byte for byte Spectra (1296 files, 143 GB) identical, 1296 of 1296 Spectral tables (2) identical, byte for byte Numbers of the paper (243) 243 of 243 in agreement Figures of the paper (5) the same images, pixel by pixel

The check found two numbers that had been rounded twice in the text. The scatter of the velocity changes of the HARPS-N flares is 0.40 m/s, not 0.41, and the excess of Appendix C is 0.43 ± 0.10 m/s, not 0.44 ± 0.11. Both are corrected.

On 22 November 2026 it was run on Linux in two ways. The reproduce workflow of the repository ran it on GitHub from the public archives, with ten spectra of the sample, in six minutes. The 12 inputs and the ten extracts are identical. On Ubuntu 24.04 with Python 3.12 the whole analysis, the spectral part included, was run on the 1296 extracts. In both, the 243 numbers agree and every table has the same numbers. The largest difference is in the eleventh significant digit. The five figures drawn on Linux are the same images as those of the paper.

The run on Linux found one defect, now corrected. The depth and the width of the mean line come from an iterative fit, which stopped within a few hundredths of a part per million of its minimum, at a point that depended on the machine. The two machines differed by up to 0.0001 ppm in those two columns of spectral_response.csv, and the command reported the table as DIFFERENT. The fit is now carried to convergence, and the two machines agree to the last digits that the arithmetic keeps. The change moved those two columns by less than 0.0001 ppm, against errors of 50 to 80 ppm, so spectral_response.csv is no longer byte for byte the table of the first run. No number of the paper and no figure changed. Run again on Windows with the corrected fit, the 16 tables are identical to those of the repository. The spectra were not downloaded a second time, because the extracts are the same files.

On 23 November 2026 a last review of the paper added twelve numbers, and the command now checks 255. They are the measurement without the flares that start soon after another one (four new rows in cleaning_variants.csv), the number of controls of a flare, and what the paper derives from the brightening of flares in visible light. The same review made the probability of detecting a shift use the shift as it is measured back, as the injections of NEID already did, and that number of the paper went from 99 to 98 %. Run again on Windows with the data on disk, the 16 tables are identical to those of the repository and the 255 numbers agree.

On 24 November 2026, the day the paper was submitted, version 1.0.0 was checked as it is archived at Zenodo. The archive is identical, file by file, to the tag of the repository. Installed from it in an empty folder, the 122 tests pass and the 255 numbers agree. On Ubuntu 24.04 with Python 3.12 the whole analysis on the data of the paper, the spectral part included, ends with Reproduced. and every table has the same numbers. On Windows, with the frozen copy of the data, the 16 tables are identical to those of the repository. A download from the public archives made that day no longer gave the inputs of the paper, because NOAA had reissued the GOES files. The reissue of the GOES files describes it.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
reproduce runs these commands in this order. Each can be run alone, and then it writes to results/.

python -m flinch download
python -m flinch coverage
python -m flinch replication
python -m flinch replication --cleaning
python -m flinch robustness
python -m flinch pilot
python -m flinch numbers
python -m flinch paper-spectra
python -m flinch chromosphere
python -m flinch paper-figures --out figures
python -m flinch verify
Output Made by Content results/flare_sample.csv coverage The 2122 M and X flares and their coverage by NEID results/velocity_by_instrument.csv replication Mean change, shift of an X1 flare and rotation term, by class and instrument, and both together (Table 1) results/replication_events.csv replication Every flare and control of both instruments, with its velocity change (Fig. 3) results/replication_profiles.csv replication Mean velocity around the peak in 10-minute bins (Fig. 2) results/early_window.csv replication Mean velocity from 60 to 50 minutes before the peak, by class and instrument (Appendix C) results/cleaning_variants.csv replication --cleaning The mean change and the rotation term with other thresholds for dropping days and, for HARPS-N, with the quality flag above 0.9 results/robustness.csv robustness The table of variants with NEID (Table A.1) results/injections.csv robustness A shift added and measured back with NEID (Appendix A) results/pilot_*.csv pilot The first NEID analysis, including the oscillation power results/text_numbers.csv numbers The counts and descriptive numbers of the text: velocities and days, what the cuts remove, the tests of a fair sample, the flare rate and the time in flare data/spectra/ paper-spectra The extracts of the 1296 spectra of the paper, each checked against its fingerprint results/spectral_response.csv chromosphere Response of every flare and control, with its errors (Table B.1) results/spectral_indices.csv chromosphere Summary of each index by class band (Table 2) PDF files paper-figures The example of the method, the mean velocity around the peak, the change of each flare against class and position, and the mean response of the spectra results/paper_check.csv verify Every number of the paper against the tables

Three environment variables move things. FLINCH_DATA is the folder of the downloads (data/ by default), FLINCH_RESULTS that of the tables (results/), and FLINCH_DATA_END the last day of data (see below).

docs.title: What is fixed, and how
docs.text:
Four things made the results depend on the day and on the machine. They are now fixed in the code.

  • The last day of data. The NEID table grows every clear day and the GOES lists are reissued with a later end date, so a later download had more flares, more observations and other controls. DATA_END in flinch/config.py is 13 November 2026. Flares and observations from that day on are ignored, whatever the download holds. The last NEID observation of the paper is of 12 November 2026.
  • The spectra. They were fetched with campaign, which works through the flares from the strongest down until a budget of hours and files runs out. What it fetches depends on the connection and on the day. flinch/reference/spectra_files.csv lists the 1296 files that it fetched for the paper, with the fingerprint of each extract, and paper-spectra fetches exactly those.
  • The random choices. Controls and bootstrap use a fixed seed.
  • The numbers of the text. Counts, percentages and tests that were not in any table are now written by numbers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
What follows can still make a reproduction differ, or makes it expensive.

  • The archives can change the data. NEID can reprocess its spectra with a newer pipeline (the 1296 used here are all of version 1.5.3), and NOAA reissues the GOES files, as it did in November 2026. The fingerprints do not prevent a change, but they detect it. The report then says which input is different, and a table that differs has an explanation. A frozen copy of the GOES files, of the NEID table and of the extracts of the 1296 spectra, as they were when the paper was computed, is attached to release 1.0.0 of the repository (flinch-data.zip, 556 MB). The reissue of the GOES files says how to repeat the paper with it, without the 143 GB.
  • The spectra are 143 GB. A level-2 file is 113 MB and the archive does not serve parts of a file, so each one is downloaded whole, reduced to an extract of 0.2 MB and deleted. The 1296 files took 3 hours and 14 minutes here, at 12 MB per second, which is 9 seconds per file. A slower line needs more in proportion. They need 400 MB of free disk at a time and leave 260 MB of extracts. A home connection may slow down after tens of GB. In the first campaign it fell to a tenth of its speed after 100 GB. In this second download it did not. The computer must stay awake, so a laptop should be plugged in and should not sleep when the lid closes. Level 2 is the cheap alternative. It does not repeat the spectral analysis, but it shows that the archive and the extraction still give the same extracts.
  • Some spectra cannot be read. For 51 exposures of two windows (27 of the X1.3 flare of 4 July 2026 and 24 of the control of the X4.9 flare of 31 December 2023) the archive serves files without the stitched spectrum. They are not in the list, and those two windows have fewer spectra than the others. That flare and that control are not among the usable ones.
  • The choice of the spectra is not repeated. The list records which spectra were fetched, not a rule that gives them again. The windows are the 20 X-class flares that NEID observed at the peak or during the rise, the same hours on the nearest flare-free day for 14 of them, and the 11 of the 25 flares between M5 and M9 that had a steady clear sky. Within a window, every spectrum near the flare was taken and one in two or three farther away. Running campaign again would not give the same files, because its budget cut the last window short and the two windows above lost spectra.
  • Software versions and machines. With the versions of requirements-lock.txt on Windows 11 the tables come out identical, byte by byte. On Linux the same versions give the same numbers to eleven significant digits, but not the same text, because another processor and other mathematical libraries round the last digits differently. Tables are therefore compared number by number, not only as text, and the report says same numbers. On Linux the extraction was checked on ten spectra taken from the archive, and the spectral analysis on the 1296 extracts made on Windows. The download of the 143 GB has not been repeated there. macOS has not been tried. NumPy does not promise the same random numbers in every future version. If they changed, the controls drawn and the bootstrap errors would change in their last digits.
  • Figures are not compared by the command. They are drawn again from the new tables. For the runs described above, on Windows and on Linux, they were turned into images and compared with those of the paper, and the five are the same pixel by pixel. With other versions of Matplotlib or other fonts they can differ in details that do not change what they show.
  • Numbers taken from other papers (the brightening of two flares in visible light and the factor of the old GOES scale) are written in flinch/verify.py as they were read in those papers. What the paper derives from them is checked. The papers themselves are not read by the command.

docs.title: The reissue of the GOES files
docs.text:
Between 22 and 24 November 2026 NOAA reissued the GOES files that the paper uses. The download of 21 and 22 November still gave the files of the paper. A download made since then does not.

Four things changed, up to the last day of data of the paper.

  • The list of flares is the same. It has the same 2187 flares of class M and X, with the same times and classes.
  • The heliographic longitude and latitude of the flares moved by 180 degrees, in about 1960 of them. In the earlier files most latitudes lay outside the range from −90 to 90 degrees, and in the reissued files none does, so the earlier values were wrong. The analysis does not depend on them. It uses the position on the disc, the Carrington longitude and differences of latitude. The columns lon and lat of results/flare_sample.csv and results/pilot_flares.csv come from the earlier files and should not be used as heliographic coordinates.
  • The one-minute X-ray fluxes of GOES-18 between 9 October and 11 November 2026 changed by up to 14 %.
  • The peak flux and the fluence of about a dozen flares changed by a few parts in a million.

This is what python -m flinch reproduce reports with a download of 24 November 2026.

What Result Inputs of the velocity analysis (12 files) 10 identical. The GOES list of M and X flares and the GOES-18 one-minute fluxes of 2026 are different Velocity tables (14) 9 identical or with the same numbers. 5 are DIFFERENT Numbers of the paper (255) 255 of 255 in agreement Figures of the velocity analysis (3) the same images, pixel by pixel Last line Not fully reproduced, and the command ends with code 1

Of the five tables that differ, flare_sample.csv and pilot_flares.csv do so in the columns lon and lat and, by less than one part in 100 000, in the fluence and the position of a few flares. velocity_by_instrument.csv and robustness.csv differ by 0.000000002 m/s at most, in the rotation term and in the shift of an X1 flare, and pilot_tests.csv by as little in one test statistic.

To get the tables of the paper exactly, use the frozen copy. Unpack flinch-data.zip in the folder of the code, which gives data/. Then fetch the HARPS-N series alone, which is a fixed release with a DOI and is not copied, and run the analysis on what is on disk.

python -c "from flinch import harpsn; harpsn.download_series()"
python -m flinch reproduce --no-download --spectra all

Do not run python -m flinch download in that folder. Since the reissue it also fetches the new flare lists of GOES-18, whose file names carry a later end date, and the code reads the latest list that it finds in data/goes/. Earlier versions of this page recommended that command. Run as above on 24 November 2026, with version 1.0.0 as archived at Zenodo, the 16 tables are identical to those of the repository and the last line is Reproduced.

python -m pytest -m network   # 2 tests: the archives still answer as the code expects

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Status: November 2026. The velocity is measured with two instruments, NEID and HARPS-N. The spectra are those of NEID: 23 flares and nine flare-free control windows.

docs.title: The velocity of the Sun does not change during flares
docs.text:
Two instruments that watched different flares give the same answer.

Change of the velocity during the flare, minus that of its controls, in m/s (in brackets, the number of flares):

NEID HARPS-N Both 95 % limit Mean change, all M and X flares −0.035 ± 0.035 (139) −0.021 ± 0.039 (115) −0.029 ± 0.026 (254) 0.07 Mean change, M class −0.032 ± 0.039 (128) −0.015 ± 0.042 (108) −0.025 ± 0.028 (236) 0.07 Mean change, X class −0.060 ± 0.088 (11) −0.104 ± 0.127 (7) −0.074 ± 0.072 (18) 0.19 Shift of an X1 flare, S −0.010 ± 0.061 −0.005 ± 0.040 −0.006 ± 0.033 0.06 Rotation term, R −0.106 ± 0.082 +0.022 ± 0.043 −0.006 ± 0.038 0.07

Together the mean change is below 0.07 m/s, less than the 0.09 m/s that the Earth imprints on the Sun. The 254 measurements are of 253 different flares: one was observed by both instruments. The data give no evidence that the flares used differ from the rest of the M and X flares. Their classes and their positions on the disc are distributed like those of the full list, with Kolmogorov-Smirnov probabilities between 0.04 and 0.96 in the eight tests (class, two coordinates on the disc and distance from its centre, for each instrument). The lowest is not unusual for the smallest of eight tests. With as few flares as in the X-class row, the error is itself uncertain by a quarter.

Three further checks give the same answer:

  • Larger flares do not shift the velocity more. For the 18 flares of class X no change is found either, but the limit, 0.19 m/s, is twice the signal of the Earth.
  • There are no shifts of opposite sign that cancel in the mean. The changes of the flares scatter as much as those of the controls: 0.40 m/s for both with NEID, 0.40 and 0.41 with HARPS-N.
  • There is no rotation signature. The rotation term is below 0.07 m/s for an X1 flare at the limb, which means K · ΔF / F < 3.7 × 10⁻⁵ per X1 flare (see Method).

docs.title: The result does not depend on the choices
docs.text:
With NEID, where the choices were made (HARPS-N was analysed afterwards, once, with them). All in m/s:

Variant Flares Mean change Shift of an X1 flare Rotation term Default 139 −0.035 ± 0.035 −0.010 ± 0.061 −0.106 ± 0.082 Daily trend: polynomial of degree 1 137 −0.022 ± 0.036 −0.015 ± 0.060 −0.045 ± 0.080 Daily trend: polynomial of degree 3 139 −0.001 ± 0.033 +0.016 ± 0.049 −0.079 ± 0.083 "During" window: 3 min either side of the steepest X-ray rise 120 −0.009 ± 0.042 −0.019 ± 0.061 −0.108 ± 0.135 "During" window: first 10 min from the start 134 −0.040 ± 0.035 +0.006 ± 0.045 −0.004 ± 0.080 "During" window: 5 min either side of the X-ray peak 126 −0.021 ± 0.042 −0.111 ± 0.085 −0.134 ± 0.154 Background: straight line fitted on both sides of the flare 93 −0.008 ± 0.040 −0.032 ± 0.070 −0.002 ± 0.113 Errors: resampling 81 active regions instead of 111 days 139 −0.035 ± 0.035 −0.010 ± 0.061 −0.106 ± 0.082

Flares that follow one another do not change it either. Without the 36 flares that start less than 45 minutes after the peak of another M or X flare, the mean change of the other 218, with both instruments, is −0.033 ± 0.029 m/s.

docs.title: A signal would have been seen
docs.text:
A shift added to the NEID velocities, and the shift measured back:

Added Measured Probability of detecting it at 95 % 5 cm/s 4.9 cm/s 40 % 10 cm/s 9.8 cm/s 88 % 20 cm/s 19.5 cm/s 100 % 50 cm/s 48.8 cm/s 100 %

With HARPS-N the same test measures back 98 %. The probability of detection is that of measuring more than 1.645 times the error, the one-sided threshold of 95 % confidence, when the shift is the one measured back. With the two instruments together, a shift of 10 cm/s common to all flares would have been detected with a probability of 98 %.

docs.title: The same spectra do see the flares
docs.text:
A result of "nothing happens" needs the proof that the instrument was looking. The spectra give it: the chromospheric lines brighten as the X-ray flux rises, peak a few minutes after the X-ray peak and are still bright 40 minutes later. In the control windows they stay flat, and in those same spectra the velocity does not move.

Mean response of the flares on the disc (within 0.9 solar radii of the centre), from 8 minutes before the X-ray peak to 10 minutes after it:

X class (8 flares) M5 to M9 (6 flares) Controls (9 windows) Ca II H and K (parts per thousand) +5.3 ± 1.7 +2.2 ± 0.4 0.0 ± 0.2 H alpha core (parts per thousand) +3.3 ± 1.1 +2.0 ± 0.2 −0.1 ± 0.2 Velocity (m/s) −0.11 ± 0.21 −0.10 ± 0.11 +0.07 ± 0.27
  • All 14 flares on the disc brighten in both lines.
  • Smaller flares respond less: those between M5 and M9, about half as much as those of class X.
  • Near the limb the response is weaker: +1.7 ± 0.9 in Ca II H and K for four X-class flares, +1.4 ± 0.5 for five between M5 and M9.
  • Weaker flares were not fetched. Between M2 and M5 the response of one flare would be below the noise, and these 14 already show that the spectra see the flares.

The table flare by flare is results/spectral_response.csv. One flare in detail, the X6.3 of 22 February 2024, whose peak came just after the last solar spectrum of that day:

docs.title: What was to be expected
docs.text:
• How bright is a flare in visible light? At the peak of an average M2 flare the Sun brightens by 7 parts per million, and in the X17 flare of 28 October 2003 it brightened by 264 (Kretzschmar 2011). Those classes are on the old GOES scale, which carried a factor 0.7; on the scale used here they give 11 to 23 parts per million for an X1 flare. The two agree within a factor of two although the flares differ by a factor of almost ninety in class: on average the visible brightening grows with the X-ray class, though not flare by flare.
  • How much does that light move the velocity? At most 2 to 4 cm/s for an X1 flare at the limb (K = 1), and less elsewhere.
  • How close do we get? The limit of the two instruments together is 1.6 to 3.5 times that. The absence of a rotation signal is what the physics predicts; it is now measured.
  • And the lines of the flaring area itself? In resolved images they are shifted by up to 200 m/s (Saar et al. 2018). A ten-thousandth of the disc shifted by 100 m/s moves the velocity of the whole Sun by about 1 cm/s, so this effect depends on the area of the flare, which has not been estimated here. The limit on the mean change bounds it from the data.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
Solar flares do not significantly contaminate the detection of Earth analogues by radial velocity, for two reasons:

  • They move the velocity very little: less than 7 cm/s on average for M and X flares together. For class X alone no change is found either, but the limit is about 20 cm/s, twice the signal of the Earth.
  • They take up little of the time. Between December 2020 and November 2026, six years that span the rise and the maximum of cycle 25, the Sun produced 358 flares of class M or X per year on average, 18 of them of class X. Counting each flare from its start to its end in the GOES list (19 minutes in the median), the Sun spent 1.6 % of the time in one of them (0.1 % for class X). In 2024, the most active year, there were 934 flares, 52 of them of class X, and the Sun spent 3.8 % of the time in one (0.3 % for class X).

This has been shown for the Sun, not for Sun-like stars in general: stars more active than the Sun, with larger and more frequent flares, are another matter.

docs.title: How this compares with published work
docs.text:
• Velocity. Pietrow et al. (2024) followed two X-class flares of 6 September 2017 with HARPS-N. They could not claim a detection: they set an upper limit of 50 cm/s and asked for a statistical follow-up. Here the mean change of 253 flares seen by two instruments is below 7 cm/s. The larger of their two flares is in the HARPS-N sample: its change is −0.01 m/s, with a single-flare error of 0.41 m/s.
  • Chromosphere. In the same two flares Ca II H and K rose by more than 1 %. Here Ca II H and K is also the most sensitive index, up to 1.7 %.
  • Light of the whole disc. The H alpha studies with imaging spectrographs (Otsu et al. 2022, 2024; Ma et al. 2024) integrate a region around the flare and normalise by the disc. NEID records the response in the light of the whole disc, and the control windows give its noise floor.

docs.title: An excess before the X-class flares of NEID that HARPS-N does not see
docs.text: In the ten minutes from 60 to 50 minutes before the X-ray peak, the X-class flares observed by NEID sit 0.43 ± 0.10 m/s above the trend of their day (19 flares with data at that time, 17 of them positive). It was noticed in the mean velocities, not predicted. It is absent in the M-class flares of NEID (0.00 ± 0.03 m/s) and in the controls, and HARPS-N does not show it: −0.12 ± 0.11 m/s for its ten X-class flares, which are other flares. The origin of the feature is unclear. If it were a general property of X-class flares, the HARPS-N sample should show it too; its absence there points to the instrument or to chance, although a solar origin cannot be excluded.

docs.title: Flares do not raise the amplitude of the solar oscillations
docs.text:
Quantity Flares Null samples 95 % limit on the excess ln(power after / before) −0.068 0.001 ± 0.053 0.16 The same, weighting high frequencies −0.013 −0.009 ± 0.060 0.10

With NEID, a mean increase above 8 % in amplitude is ruled out. This tests the proposal of Karoff and Kjeldsen (2008), with the limitation that the 83 s cadence reaches only 6 mHz.

docs.title: What is left
docs.text: • A third instrument, to see whether the excess before the X-class flares is a feature of NEID.

def flux_to_class(flux: float) -> str:
    """Peak flux in W m^-2 to GOES class."""
    for letter in "XMCB":
        if flux >= _CLASS_BASE[letter]:
            return f"{letter}{flux / _CLASS_BASE[letter]:.1f}"
    return f"A{flux / _CLASS_BASE['A']:.1f}"

def find_product_url(satellite: int, product: str) -> str:
    """URL of the mission-long file of a product (the file name carries its end date)."""
    directory = product_directory(satellite, product)
    pattern = rf'href="(sci_xrsf-l2-{product}_g\d\d_s\d{{8}}_e\d{{8}}_v[\d-]+\.nc)"'
    names = re.findall(pattern, fetch_text(directory))

docs.title: read_flloc
docs.text:
read_flloc(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame

Read a flare location file: one row per flare_id with its position on the disc.

x_norm and y_norm are helioprojective coordinates in units of the solar radius (x positive towards the west limb, the receding one). r_norm is the distance to the disc centre. Positions come from the quadrant diode of the X-ray sensor and are unreliable for weak flares; entries without a position are NaN. car_lon is the Carrington longitude, which stays fixed for a region as the Sun rotates.

Source code in flinch/goes.py 
def read_flloc(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a flare location file: one row per ``flare_id`` with its position on the disc.

    ``x_norm`` and ``y_norm`` are helioprojective coordinates in units of the solar radius
    (x positive towards the west limb, the receding one). ``r_norm`` is the distance to the disc
    centre. Positions come from the quadrant diode of the X-ray sensor and are unreliable for
    weak flares; entries without a position are NaN. ``car_lon`` is the Carrington longitude,
    which stays fixed for a region as the Sun rotates.
    """
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as handle:
        xy = handle["flloc_xy"][:].astype(float)
        radius = handle["solar_radius"][:].astype(float)
        hg = handle["flloc_hg"][:].astype(float)
        carrington = handle["flloc_car"][:].astype(float)
        flare_id = handle["flare_id"][:]
    xy[xy < -9000.0] = np.nan
    hg[hg < -9000.0] = np.nan
    carrington[carrington < -9000.0] = np.nan
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "flare_id": flare_id,
            "x_norm": xy[:, 0] / radius,
            "y_norm": xy[:, 1] / radius,
            "lon": hg[:, 0],
            "lat": hg[:, 1],
            "car_lon": carrington[:, 0],
        }
    )
    table["r_norm"] = np.hypot(table["x_norm"], table["y_norm"])
    return table.drop_duplicates("flare_id")

docs.title: read_flsum
docs.text:
read_flsum(path: Path, satellite: int | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Read a flare summary file into one row per flare.

The file stores one record per event marker (start, peak, end) sharing a flare_id. Times are Julian dates (UTC); fluxes are in W m^-2 (1-8 Angstrom), fluences in J m^-2.

Source code in flinch/goes.py 
def read_flsum(path: Path, satellite: int | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a flare summary file into one row per flare.

    The file stores one record per event marker (start, peak, end) sharing a ``flare_id``.
    Times are Julian dates (UTC); fluxes are in W m^-2 (1-8 Angstrom), fluences in J m^-2.
    """
    path = Path(path)
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as handle:
        records = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "jd": JD_J2000 + handle["time"][:] / 86400.0,
                "status": handle["status"].asstr()[:],
                "goes_class": handle["flare_class"].asstr()[:],
                "flux": handle["xrsb_flux"][:].astype(float),
                "fluence": handle["integrated_flux"][:].astype(float),
                "flare_id": handle["flare_id"][:],
            }
        )
    if satellite is None:
        match = re.search(r"_g(\d\d)_", path.name)
        satellite = int(match.group(1)) if match else 0

    def marker(status: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        return records[records["status"] == status].drop_duplicates("flare_id").set_index("flare_id")

    peaks, starts, ends = marker("EVENT_PEAK"), marker("EVENT_START"), marker("EVENT_END")
    peaks = peaks[peaks["goes_class"] != ""]
    flares = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "jd_start": starts["jd"].reindex(peaks.index),
            "jd_peak": peaks["jd"],
            "jd_end": ends["jd"].reindex(peaks.index),
            "goes_class": peaks["goes_class"],
            "peak_flux": peaks["flux"],
            "fluence": ends["fluence"].reindex(peaks.index),
        }
    )
    flares["satellite"] = satellite
    return flares.reset_index().sort_values("jd_peak", ignore_index=True)

docs.title: merge_flare_lists
docs.text:
merge_flare_lists(primary: DataFrame, secondary: DataFrame, tolerance_min: float = 3.0) -> pd.DataFrame

The primary list plus the flares of the secondary with no counterpart in the primary.

Two entries are the same flare when their peaks are closer than tolerance_min minutes, or when the secondary peak falls between the start and the end of a primary flare (the two satellites can place the peak of a long, flat flare several minutes apart).

Source code in flinch/goes.py 
def merge_flare_lists(primary: pd.DataFrame, secondary: pd.DataFrame, tolerance_min: float = 3.0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The primary list plus the flares of the secondary with no counterpart in the primary.

    Two entries are the same flare when their peaks are closer than ``tolerance_min`` minutes,
    or when the secondary peak falls between the start and the end of a primary flare (the two
    satellites can place the peak of a long, flat flare several minutes apart).
    """
    if primary.empty or secondary.empty:
        return pd.concat([primary, secondary], ignore_index=True).sort_values("jd_peak", ignore_index=True)
    peaks = np.sort(primary["jd_peak"].to_numpy())
    candidates = secondary["jd_peak"].to_numpy()
    index = np.searchsorted(peaks, candidates)
    before = np.abs(candidates - peaks[np.clip(index - 1, 0, len(peaks) - 1)])
    after = np.abs(peaks[np.clip(index, 0, len(peaks) - 1)] - candidates)
    isolated = np.minimum(before, after) > tolerance_min * MINUTE
    if {"jd_start", "jd_end"} <= set(primary.columns):
        windows = primary.dropna(subset=["jd_start", "jd_end"]).sort_values("jd_start")
        if not windows.empty:
            starts, ends = windows["jd_start"].to_numpy(), windows["jd_end"].to_numpy()
            last_started = np.searchsorted(starts, candidates, side="right") - 1
            inside = (last_started >= 0) & (candidates <= ends[np.clip(last_started, 0, len(ends) - 1)])
            isolated &= ~inside
    merged = pd.concat([primary, secondary[isolated]], ignore_index=True)
    return merged.sort_values("jd_peak", ignore_index=True)

docs.title: load_flares
docs.text:
load_flares(directory: Path | None = None, satellites: tuple[int, ...] = SATELLITES) -> pd.DataFrame

Merged flare list from the downloaded summaries (run python -m flinch download first).

Source code in flinch/goes.py 
def load_flares(directory: Path | None = None, satellites: tuple[int, ...] = SATELLITES) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Merged flare list from the downloaded summaries (run ``python -m flinch download`` first)."""
    directory = Path(directory or data_dir() / "goes")
    merged = None
    for satellite in satellites:
        files = sorted(directory.glob(f"sci_xrsf-l2-flsum_g{satellite}_*.nc"))
        if not files:
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"no GOES-{satellite} flare summary in {directory}; run `python -m flinch download`"
            )
        flares = read_flsum(files[-1])
        locations = sorted(directory.glob(f"sci_xrsf-l2-flloc_g{satellite}_*.nc"))
        if locations:
            flares = flares.merge(read_flloc(locations[-1]), on="flare_id", how="left")
        merged = flares if merged is None else merge_flare_lists(merged, flares)
    # The lists are reissued with a later end date: keep the same flares whatever the download.
    merged = merged[merged["jd_peak"] < data_end_jd()].reset_index(drop=True)
    merged["peak"] = jd_to_datetime(merged["jd_peak"])
    return merged

def load_avg1m(satellite: int, year: int, directory: Path | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Julian dates and 1-8 Angstrom fluxes (W m^-2) at one-minute cadence; downloaded if missing."""
    directory = Path(directory or data_dir() / "goes")
    files = sorted(directory.glob(f"sci_xrsf-l2-avg1m_g{satellite}_y{year}_*.nc"))
    path = files[-1] if files else download(avg1m_url(satellite, year), directory / avg1m_url(satellite, year).rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as handle:
        jd = JD_J2000 + handle["time"][:] / 86400.0
        flux = handle["xrsb_flux"][:].astype(float)
    flux[~(flux > 0.0)] = np.nan  # fill values and gaps
    return jd, flux

Download the yearly one-minute files that add_impulsive_time needs for these flares.

def download_avg1m(flares: pd.DataFrame, directory: Path | None = None) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Download the yearly one-minute files that ``add_impulsive_time`` needs for these flares.

    Returns the (satellite, year) pairs. A year that the archive does not hold is skipped, as
    ``add_impulsive_time`` does.
    """
    years = jd_to_datetime(flares["jd_peak"]).year
    pairs = sorted({(int(satellite), int(year)) for satellite, year in zip(flares["satellite"], years)})
    done = []
    for satellite, year in pairs:
        try:
            load_avg1m(satellite, year, directory)
            done.append((satellite, year))
        except RuntimeError:  # no file for that year
            continue
    return done

docs.title: add_impulsive_time
docs.text:
add_impulsive_time(flares: DataFrame, directory: Path | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Add jd_impulsive: the time of the steepest rise of the X-ray flux of each flare.

The time derivative of the soft X-ray flux follows the energy deposition by accelerated particles (the Neupert effect), so its maximum marks the impulsive phase better than the X-ray peak, which comes minutes later. It is searched between the start and the peak with a centred difference over two minutes; flares without one-minute data keep NaN.

Source code in flinch/goes.py 
def add_impulsive_time(flares: pd.DataFrame, directory: Path | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add ``jd_impulsive``: the time of the steepest rise of the X-ray flux of each flare.

    The time derivative of the soft X-ray flux follows the energy deposition by accelerated
    particles (the Neupert effect), so its maximum marks the impulsive phase better than the
    X-ray peak, which comes minutes later. It is searched between the start and the peak with a
    centred difference over two minutes; flares without one-minute data keep NaN.
    """
    out = flares.copy()
    out["jd_impulsive"] = np.nan
    start = out["jd_start"].fillna(out["jd_peak"] - 10.0 * MINUTE)
    years = jd_to_datetime(out["jd_peak"]).year
    for (satellite, year), rows in out.groupby([out["satellite"], years]):
        try:
            jd, flux = load_avg1m(int(satellite), int(year), directory)
        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001  (a missing year leaves NaN)
            continue
        slope = np.full(len(flux), np.nan)
        slope[1:-1] = (flux[2:] - flux[:-2]) / 2.0
        for index in rows.index:
            first, last = np.searchsorted(jd, [start[index] - 0.5 * MINUTE, out.at[index, "jd_peak"] + 0.5 * MINUTE])
            if last - first >= 2 and np.any(np.isfinite(slope[first:last])):
                out.at[index, "jd_impulsive"] = jd[first + int(np.nanargmax(slope[first:last]))] + 0.5 * MINUTE
    return out

def parse_csv(text: str, expected_column: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Parse a CSV answer of the archive; raise if it is an error message instead of a table."""
    header = [name.strip().strip('"').lower() for name in text.split("\n", 1)[0].split(",")]
    if expected_column.lower() not in header:
        raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected answer from the NEID archive: {text[:300]!r}")
    return pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text), low_memory=False)

def download_solar_table(
    destination: Path | None = None, last_year: int | None = None, overwrite: bool = False
) -> Path:
    """Download the table of all solar observations (one query per year); returns the local path."""
    destination = Path(destination or data_dir() / "neid" / "neid_solar_l2.csv.gz")
    if destination.exists() and not overwrite:
        return destination
    last_year = last_year or dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).year
    end = data_end_jd()  # the table grows every clear day: nothing is asked beyond the last day of data
    columns = ", ".join(COLUMNS)
    chunks = []
    for year in range(FIRST_YEAR, last_year + 1):
        first, last = year_start_jd(year), min(year_start_jd(year + 1), end)
        if first >= last:
            break
        adql = f"select {columns} from {SOLAR_TABLE} where obsjd >= {first} and obsjd < {last} order by obsjd"
        chunks.append(query(adql, "obsjd"))
    table = pd.concat([chunk for chunk in chunks if not chunk.empty], ignore_index=True)
    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    table.to_csv(destination, index=False)
    return destination

def read_solar_table(path: Path | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read the downloaded table, sorted in time, with the velocity also in m/s (``rv_ms``)."""
    path = Path(path or data_dir() / "neid" / "neid_solar_l2.csv.gz")
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{path} not found; run `python -m flinch download`")
    table = pd.read_csv(path, low_memory=False)
    table = table[table["obsjd"] < data_end_jd()].sort_values("obsjd", ignore_index=True)
    table["rv_ms"] = table["ccfrvmod"] * 1000.0
    table["rv_err_ms"] = table["dvrms"] * 1000.0
    return table

def class_band(goes_class: str) -> str:

docs.text:
add_coverage(flares: DataFrame, observation_jd, peak_tolerance_min: float = 2.0, baseline_min: float = 30.0, min_points: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame

Add coverage columns to a flare table.

n_peak: observations within peak_tolerance_min of the flare peak. n_pre: observations in the baseline_min minutes before the flare start. n_post: observations in the baseline_min minutes after the peak. at_peak: the instrument was observing at the peak. well_covered: at the peak, with at least min_points observations before and after.

A flare without a recorded start is assumed to start 10 minutes before its peak.

Source code in flinch/coverage.py 
def add_coverage(
    flares: pd.DataFrame,
    observation_jd,
    peak_tolerance_min: float = 2.0,
    baseline_min: float = 30.0,
    min_points: int = 5,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add coverage columns to a flare table.

    ``n_peak``: observations within ``peak_tolerance_min`` of the flare peak.
    ``n_pre``: observations in the ``baseline_min`` minutes before the flare start.
    ``n_post``: observations in the ``baseline_min`` minutes after the peak.
    ``at_peak``: the instrument was observing at the peak.
    ``well_covered``: at the peak, with at least ``min_points`` observations before and after.

    A flare without a recorded start is assumed to start 10 minutes before its peak.
    """
    times = np.sort(np.asarray(observation_jd, dtype=float))
    out = flares.copy()
    peak = out["jd_peak"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    start = out["jd_start"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    start = np.where(np.isfinite(start), start, peak - 10.0 * MINUTE)
    out["n_peak"] = count_between(times, peak - peak_tolerance_min * MINUTE, peak + peak_tolerance_min * MINUTE)
    out["n_pre"] = count_between(times, start - baseline_min * MINUTE, start)
    out["n_post"] = count_between(times, peak, peak + baseline_min * MINUTE)
    out["at_peak"] = out["n_peak"] > 0
    out["well_covered"] = out["at_peak"] & (out["n_pre"] >= min_points) & (out["n_post"] >= min_points)
    return out

def summarize(flares: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Number of flares per class band: total, observed at the peak, and well covered."""
    bands = flares["goes_class"].map(class_band)
    rows = []
    for band in BANDS:
        selected = flares[bands == band]
        rows.append(
            {
                "band": band,
                "total": len(selected),
                "at_peak": int(selected["at_peak"].sum()),
                "well_covered": int(selected["well_covered"].sum()),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def data_end_jd() -> float:
    """Julian date (UTC) from which flares and observations are ignored.

    ``DATA_END`` by default. The environment variable ``FLINCH_DATA_END`` replaces it with
    another date (``2027-06-01``) or lifts the limit (``none``), to extend the study; the
    numbers of the paper are then no longer reproduced.
    """
    text = os.environ.get("FLINCH_DATA_END", DATA_END).strip()
    if text.lower() in ("", "none"):
        return float("inf")
    since_1970 = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(text) - dt.datetime(1970, 1, 1)
    return since_1970.total_seconds() / 86400.0 + 2440587.5

def jd_to_datetime(jd):
    """Julian date(s) to pandas timestamps (UTC, timezone-naive)."""
    seconds = (np.asarray(jd, dtype=float) - JD_UNIX_EPOCH) * 86400.0
    if seconds.ndim == 0:

    return pd.to_datetime(seconds, unit="s")

docs.title: flinch.reproduce
docs.text:
Reproduce the paper from the public archives, in one command, and report what agrees.

python -m flinch reproduce downloads the data, runs every step of the analysis, compares each new table with the one kept in the repository and checks every number of the paper against the new tables. The steps are the ordinary commands of the package, run one after another; this module only puts them in order, times them and writes the report. The new tables go to their own folder, so the repository is left as it was.

The spectra are the expensive part: 1296 files of 113 MB that the archive serves whole, 143 GB in all. They are left out by default. --spectra sample fetches a few of them and compares each with the fingerprint of the one used in the paper; --spectra all fetches them all and repeats the spectral analysis.

class Report:
    """Lines printed as the run goes and saved at the end."""

    def __init__(self, path: Path) -> None:

How much "one" of the measured quantity is in each column of a table.

The response of the spectra is written as a relative change, in parts per thousand or per million of each quantity. A difference of 1e-9 in the quantity is 1e-6 or 1e-3 in those columns, and that is what the comparison allows there. Every other column is in its own unit.

def column_units(name: str) -> dict[str, float]:
    """How much "one" of the measured quantity is in each column of a table.

    The response of the spectra is written as a relative change, in parts per thousand or per
    million of each quantity. A difference of 1e-9 in the quantity is 1e-6 or 1e-3 in those
    columns, and that is what the comparison allows there. Every other column is in its own unit.
    """
    if name != "spectral_response.csv":
        return {}
    from .response import QUANTITIES, SCALE

    return {column + suffix: SCALE[unit] for column, _, unit in QUANTITIES if unit in SCALE for suffix in ("", "_err", "_total_err")}

docs.text:
compare_tables(reference: Path, new: Path) -> tuple[str, str]

Compare a new table with the reference one.

Returns the verdict and a detail: "identical" (the same text), "same numbers" (every number within RELATIVE_TOLERANCE), "DIFFERENT" (with the columns that differ and by how much), or "missing".

Source code in flinch/reproduce.py 
def compare_tables(reference: Path, new: Path) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Compare a new table with the reference one.

    Returns the verdict and a detail: "identical" (the same text), "same numbers" (every number
    within ``RELATIVE_TOLERANCE``), "DIFFERENT" (with the columns that differ and by how much),
    or "missing".
    """
    units = column_units(reference.name)
    if not reference.exists() or not new.exists():
        return "missing", "no reference table" if not reference.exists() else "the step did not write it"
    if reference.read_bytes().replace(b"\r\n", b"\n") == new.read_bytes().replace(b"\r\n", b"\n"):
        return "identical", ""
    old, now = pd.read_csv(reference), pd.read_csv(new)
    if list(old.columns) != list(now.columns):
        return "DIFFERENT", "other columns"
    if len(old) != len(now):
        return "DIFFERENT", f"{len(old)} rows in the repository, {len(now)} now"
    differing = []
    for column in old.columns:
        a, b = old[column], now[column]
        if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(a) and pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(b):
            x, y = a.to_numpy(dtype=float), b.to_numpy(dtype=float)
            both = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
            if not np.array_equal(np.isfinite(x), np.isfinite(y)):
                differing.append(f"{column} (values missing in one of them)")
            elif both.any():
                gap = np.abs(x[both] - y[both])
                allowed = RELATIVE_TOLERANCE * np.maximum(units.get(column, 1.0), np.abs(x[both]))
                if np.any(gap > allowed):
                    differing.append(f"{column} (by up to {gap.max():.3g})")
        elif not a.astype(str).equals(b.astype(str)):
            differing.append(column)
    if differing:
        return "DIFFERENT", ", ".join(differing)
    return "same numbers", f"differences below {RELATIVE_TOLERANCE:g}"

def step(report: Report, out: Path, command: str, *paths: str) -> int:
    """Run ``python -m flinch <command> <paths>``, keep its output in a file and report how it went.

    The command writes its tables and figures under ``out``, not in the repository.
    """
    began = time.monotonic()
    log = out / "logs" / (command.replace(" ", "_").replace("--", "") + ".txt")
    env = dict(os.environ, FLINCH_RESULTS=str(out / "results"), FLINCH_FIGURES=str(out / "site_figures"))
    with open(log, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        done = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-m", "flinch", *command.split(), *paths], cwd=REPO_ROOT, env=env, stdout=handle, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT
        )
    seconds = time.monotonic() - began
    verdict = "done" if done.returncode == 0 else f"exit code {done.returncode}"
    report.say(f"  {command:28s} {verdict:14s} {seconds:7.0f} s   output in {log}")
    return done.returncode

def run(spectra: str = "none", sample: int = 10, download: bool = True, out: Path | None = None) -> int:
    """Run everything and write the report; returns 0 when every table and every number agrees.

    Nothing in the repository is touched: the new tables, the figures, the output of every step
    and the report go to ``out`` (``reproduction/`` by default).
    """
    from . import campaign, inputs, verify

    out = Path(out or REPO_ROOT / "reproduction").resolve()
    committed, new, figures = REPO_ROOT / "results", out / "results", out / "figures"
    for folder in (out / "logs", new, figures):
        folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    report = Report(out / "report.txt")
    files = len(campaign.paper_files())
    report.say(f"flinch reproduce, {dt.datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}")
    report.say(f"{platform.platform()}, Python {sys.version.split()[0]}, numpy {np.__version__}, pandas {pd.__version__}")
    report.say(f"Data in {data_dir()}")
    report.say(f"Last day of data: {os.environ.get('FLINCH_DATA_END', 'as in the paper')}")
    plan = {
        "none": "not fetched",
        "sample": f"{sample} files, {sample * campaign.FILE_MB / 1024:.1f} GB",
        "all": f"{files} files, {files * campaign.FILE_MB / 1024:.0f} GB",
    }[spectra]
    report.say(f"Spectra: {plan}")
    report.say()
    failures = 0

    report.say("1. Data")
    if download:
        failures += step(report, out, "download") != 0
    try:
        checked = inputs.check()
        for row in checked.itertuples():
            report.say(f"  {row.input:36s} {row.status}")
        if (checked["status"] != "identical").any():
            report.say("  Some inputs are not those of the paper: the archive has changed, and the tables below may differ for that reason.")
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001  (no data: the steps below say so one by one)
        report.say(f"  the inputs could not be read ({type(exc).__name__}: {exc})")
        failures += 1
    report.say()

    report.say("2. Velocity analysis")
    for command in VELOCITY_STEPS:
        failures += step(report, out, command) != 0
    report.say()

    report.say("3. Spectra")
    if spectra != "none":
        code = step(report, out, "paper-spectra" + (f" --sample {sample}" if spectra == "sample" else ""))
        check = data_dir() / "spectra" / "check.csv"
        if check.exists():
            counts = pd.read_csv(check)["status"].value_counts()
            report.say("  extracts compared with those of the paper: " + ", ".join(f"{number} {label}" for label, number in counts.items()))
        failures += code != 0
    recomputed = spectra_complete()
    if recomputed:
        failures += step(report, out, "chromosphere") != 0
    else:
        report.say(f"  spectral analysis not repeated: it needs the {files} spectra of the paper (--spectra all)")
        for name in SPECTRAL_TABLES:  # the check of the numbers below reads them
            if (committed / name).exists():
                shutil.copyfile(committed / name, new / name)
    report.say()

    report.say("4. Figures")
    failures += step(report, out, "paper-figures --out", str(figures)) != 0
    report.say()

    report.say("5. New tables, against those of the repository")
    different = 0
    for name in (*VELOCITY_TABLES, *SPECTRAL_TABLES):
        if name in SPECTRAL_TABLES and not recomputed:
            report.say(f"  {name:30s} not recomputed")
            continue
        verdict, detail = compare_tables(committed / name, new / name)
        different += verdict in ("DIFFERENT", "missing")
        report.say(f"  {name:30s} {verdict}" + (f": {detail}" if detail else ""))
    report.say()

    report.say("6. Numbers of the paper, against the new tables")
    table = verify.run(new)
    table.to_csv(new / "paper_check.csv", index=False)
    wrong = table[~table["ok"]]
    for row in wrong.itertuples():
        report.say(f"  NOT IN AGREEMENT  {row.where}, {row.what}: paper {row.paper}, here {row.here}")
    report.say(f"  {len(table)} numbers checked, {len(table) - len(wrong)} in agreement, {len(wrong)} not")
    if not recomputed:
        report.say("  (the numbers of the spectra were checked against the tables of the repository, not against new ones)")
    report.say()

    ok = failures == 0 and different == 0 and wrong.empty
    summary = f"Not fully reproduced: {failures} steps failed, {different} tables differ, {len(wrong)} numbers of the paper not in agreement."
    report.say("Reproduced." if ok else summary)
    report.say(f"Everything is in {out}: report.txt, results/, figures/ and logs/")
    return 0 if ok else 1

Check every number of the paper against the tables in results/.

The numbers of the paper are written down here, as printed, with the place where they appear. Each is compared with the value in the tables at the precision of the paper: a number passes when the paper gives a correct rounding of it. Run the analysis first and then this check, and the paper is verified against what the code produces today.

A growing list of comparisons between the paper and the tables.

Source code in flinch/verify.py 
class Checks:
    """A growing list of comparisons between the paper and the tables."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.rows: list[dict] = []

    def add(self, where: str, what: str, paper, here, decimals: int = 0) -> None:
        """One or several numbers (a value and its error): ``paper`` as printed, ``here`` from the tables."""
        paper = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(paper, dtype=float))
        here = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(here, dtype=float))
        ok = bool(np.all(np.isfinite(here)) and np.all(np.abs(here - paper) <= 0.5 * 10.0**-decimals + 1.0e-9))
        self.rows.append(
            {
                "where": where,
                "what": what,
                "paper": " +/- ".join(_text(value, decimals) for value in paper),
                "here": " +/- ".join("missing" if not np.isfinite(value) else _text(value, decimals + 2) for value in here),
                "ok": ok,
            }
        )

    def table(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        return pd.DataFrame(self.rows)

def velocity_checks(checks: Checks, directory: Path) -> None:
    """Table 1, the text of Sect. 4.1 and 4.2, and the appendices on robustness and on the early window."""
    table = _read(directory, "velocity_by_instrument.csv")
    if table is None:
        return _missing(checks, "Table 1", "velocity_by_instrument.csv")
    cell = table.set_index(["instrument", "band"])
    for label, band, statistic, *instruments, limit in TABLE_1:
        for name, (flares, value, error) in zip(("NEID", "HARPS-N", "Both"), instruments):
            row = cell.loc[(name, band)]
            checks.add("Table 1", f"{label}: flares, {name}", flares, row["flares"])
            checks.add("Table 1", f"{label}: value, {name}", (value, error), (row[statistic], row[f"{statistic}_err"]), 3)
        both = cell.loc[("Both", band)]
        checks.add("Table 1", f"{label}: 95 % limit", limit, abs(both[statistic]) + 1.645 * both[f"{statistic}_err"], 2)
    both = cell.loc[("Both", "M and X")]
    for name, flares, controls in (("NEID", 0.40, 0.40), ("HARPS-N", 0.40, 0.41)):
        row = cell.loc[(name, "M and X")]
        checks.add("Sect. 4.1", f"scatter of the changes of the flares, {name} (m/s)", flares, row["flare_std"], 2)
        checks.add("Sect. 4.1", f"scatter of the changes of the controls, {name} (m/s)", controls, row["control_std"], 2)
    limit = (abs(both["rotation"]) + 1.645 * both["rotation_err"]) / robust.V_LIMB_FROM_EARTH_MS
    checks.add("Eq. 9", "limit on K dF/F per X1 flare, in units of 1e-5", 3.7, limit * 1.0e5, 1)
    # What that limit is compared with: the brightening of an X1 flare on the scale of GOES-16, and the shift it gives at the limb.
    per_x1 = sorted(ppm / (flux / OLD_SCALE / 1.0e-4) for flux, ppm in BRIGHTENING)
    checks.add("Sect. 5.1", "ratio of the two brightenings of an X1 flare, about two", 2, per_x1[1] / per_x1[0])
    for label, ppm, paper_ppm, paper_shift, paper_ratio in zip(("lowest", "highest"), per_x1, (11, 23), (2, 4), (3.5, 1.6)):
        checks.add("Sect. 5.1", f"{label} brightening of an X1 flare (ppm)", paper_ppm, ppm)
        checks.add("Sect. 5.1", f"largest shift at the limb with the {label} brightening (cm/s)", paper_shift, 100.0 * ppm * 1.0e-6 * robust.V_LIMB_FROM_EARTH_MS)
        checks.add("Sect. 5.1", f"limit over the {label} brightening", paper_ratio, limit / (ppm * 1.0e-6), 1)
    for name, paper in (("NEID", 15), ("HARPS-N", 9)):
        row = cell.loc[(name, "M and X")]
        checks.add("Sect. 3.3", f"controls per flare on average, {name}", paper, row["controls"] / row["flares"])

    variants = _read(directory, "cleaning_variants.csv")
    if variants is None:
        _missing(checks, "Sect. 3.1", "cleaning_variants.csv")
    else:
        row = variants[(variants["instrument"] == "HARPS-N") & (variants["variant"] == "quality flag above 0.9") & (variants["band"] == "M and X")].iloc[0]
        checks.add("Sect. 3.1", "HARPS-N with the quality flag above 0.9: flares", 126, row["flares"])
        checks.add("Sect. 3.1", "HARPS-N with the quality flag above 0.9: mean change", (-0.005, 0.038), (row["mean"], row["mean_err"]), 3)
        # Sect. 4.2: without the flares that start less than 45 min after the peak of another one, both instruments.
        alone = variants[(variants["variant"] == replication.ISOLATED) & (variants["band"] == "M and X")]
        if len(alone) != 2:
            checks.add("Sect. 4.2", "rows of the flares not preceded by another one (cleaning_variants.csv)", 2, len(alone))
        else:
            weight = 1.0 / alone["mean_err"].to_numpy(dtype=float) ** 2
            mean = float(np.sum(weight * alone["mean"].to_numpy(dtype=float)) / np.sum(weight))
            checks.add("Sect. 4.2", "flares not preceded by another M or X flare within 45 min", 218, alone["flares"].sum())
            checks.add("Sect. 4.2", "flares preceded by another one, left out", 36, both["flares"] - alone["flares"].sum())
            checks.add("Sect. 4.2", "mean change without the flares preceded by another one", (-0.033, 0.029), (mean, 1.0 / np.sqrt(np.sum(weight))), 3)

    other = _read(directory, "robustness.csv")
    if other is None:
        _missing(checks, "Table A.1", "robustness.csv")
    else:
        for label, index, flares, mean, shift, rotation in TABLE_A1:
            row = other.iloc[index]
            checks.add("Table A.1", f"{label}: flares", flares, row["flares"])
            for name, statistic, (value, error) in (("mean change", "mean", mean), ("S", "per_X1", shift), ("R", "rotation", rotation)):
                checks.add("Table A.1", f"{label}: {name}", (value, error), (row[statistic], row[f"{statistic}_err"]), 3)
        checks.add("Table A.1", "days resampled by default", 111, other.iloc[0]["days"])
        checks.add("Table A.1", "active regions resampled instead", 81, other.iloc[8]["days"])

    injections = _read(directory, "injections.csv")
    if injections is None:
        _missing(checks, "Appendix A", "injections.csv")
    else:
        for row, recovered, probability in zip(injections.itertuples(), (4.9, 9.8, 19.5, 48.8), (40, 88, 100, 100)):
            checks.add("Appendix A", f"shift of {100 * row.injected_ms:.0f} cm/s added to NEID, measured back (cm/s)", recovered, 100.0 * row.recovered_ms, 1)
            checks.add("Appendix A", f"shift of {100 * row.injected_ms:.0f} cm/s, probability of detection with NEID (%)", probability, 100.0 * row.detection_probability)

    early = _read(directory, "early_window.csv")
    if early is None:
        _missing(checks, "Appendix C", "early_window.csv")
    else:
        row = early.set_index(["instrument", "band"])
        for name, band, flares, value in (("NEID", "X", 19, (0.43, 0.10)), ("NEID", "M", 183, (0.00, 0.03)), ("HARPS-N", "X", 10, (-0.12, 0.11))):
            chosen = row.loc[(name, band)]
            checks.add("Appendix C", f"velocity 60 to 50 min before the peak, {band} class, {name}: flares", flares, chosen["flares"])
            checks.add("Appendix C", f"velocity 60 to 50 min before the peak, {band} class, {name} (m/s)", value, (chosen["mean"], chosen["sem"]), 2)
        checks.add("Appendix C", "X-class flares of NEID above the trend in that window", 17, row.loc[("NEID", "X"), "positive"])

def text_checks(checks: Checks, directory: Path) -> None:
